newsitem.title: IRAQ: 'Are the Turks coming?' Iraqi Kurds ask.
newsitem.headline: 'Are the Turks coming?' Iraqi Kurds ask.

text.p: The rumbling of warplanes stopped all conversation in the sweltering tents and mud-brick shanties of this Iraqi Kurdish border village as men stepped out and craned their necks skyward to see if the Turks were coming.
"How can we not be afraid?" said 54-year-old Khusaba Markhae Zaja as he crouched nervously beside his one-storey hovel.
"The Turks are cruel. They have no patience, no understanding for us. So we fear them. Everyone here has been a refugee at least once. We don't want to have to start again."

Turkish troops have massed on Turkey's border with Iraq and Ankara has suggested it is preparing for a limited push into northern Iraq to root out Turkish Kurdish rebels who use the mountains there as a sanctuary from which to launch attacks.
That left Iraqi Kurds in border villages twitching like horses in a burning barn on Friday, wanting to bolt but not quite sure how or where to run.
Past incursions by Ankara targeted Turkish and Iraqi Kurds alike, and left abandoned and destroyed villages in their wake.
Ankara sent 35,000 troops 40 km (25 miles) into northern Iraq in March 1995 for a six-week incursion against the Turkey-based separatist Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK).
Jets made repeated passes over Kani Masi in the afternoon. The planes flew so high neither reporters nor villagers could see the aircraft or tell whose they were.
When the planes finally left, the 277 families in the village resumed their daily business -- eking out a precarious existence along one of the most fraught borders in the world.
"We saw two Turkish planes and a helicopter this morning and there was some bombing on the other side of the mountain last night," said Abdul Aziz, a nurse in the village.
Three kilometres (two miles) to the north, on the other side of the mountain, lies Turkey.
The land in between, stretching to hundreds of kilometres east and west, is a wild, remote no-man's land -- a smugglers paradise and rebels haven, where force is the only law.
Iraqi troops forced rebel Iraqi Kurds from their villages along this border in 1978, dynamiting every building.
Not until the West established a safe haven for Kurds in northern Iraq after the 1991 Gulf War, were Kurdish families able to return and begin rebuilding their lives.
Thanks to humanitarian aid and backbreaking hard work, villages and hamlets sprang to life once again.
Now many of those settlements are again threatened -- this time by Ankara, not Baghdad.
One such place is Tarwanish, about 10 km east of Kani Masi and just two kilometres from the Turkish border.
Turkish aircraft bombed the village on 21 March of this year, killing most of the local livestock and wounding some civilians, the Kurds say. Ankara denies targeting settlements.
Since then, Tarwanish has stood empty. Its homes and school and mosque, all rebuilt in recent years courtesy of international humanitarian aid, are abandoned.
The families who built those structures after 14 years as refugees now live in tents or branch-covered lean-tos in Kani Masi or have crowded into one of northern Iraq's teeming cities.
Amina Yusef trudged up the steep mountain path from Tarwanish to Kani Masi on Friday morning, carrying a basket of fruit and vegetables picked from a family plot inside the town.
"We go on foot, while it's still dark. And of course it's a risk because the Turks look down on the village from the mountain and might see us," the woman told Reuters.
"I have to go because I have 12 children in Kani Masi and they need this food. We want to go back home. Look at my ragged clothes. Look at how dirty I am. Nobody should live like this,"
But any new Turkish incursion seems likely to expand rather than contract the free-fire zone in which Kurds -- Turkish or Iraqi -- are considered fair game.
The worry is that Kani Masi will become the next Tarwanish.
"The Turks say they must attack because of the PKK," explained Abdul Aziz, himself a refugee from Tarwanish.
"They don't live among us. They live primitively further into the mountains. We don't see them or meet. All we want to do is live in peace."
